content: In the field of botany, the term contrayerva (or contrajerva) refers to the root and scaly rhizome of various tropical American species of the genus Dorstenia, which belong to the family Moraceae. Specifically, it includes species such as Dorstenia contrayerva and Dorstenia braziliensis. These plants are native to South America, and their aromatic roots have been historically utilized in medicine as mild stimulants and tonics. Additionally, the contrayerva root was once employed as an antidote for snake bites. In Jamaica, the name contrayerva is also used to describe a species of birthwort, Aristolochia odoratissima, which is still believed to possess antidotal properties. The root of contrayerva is smaller than that of the iris plant, with a reddish exterior and a white interior. It is characterized by a knotted and fibrous texture. For the root to be considered effective, it must be fresh, heavy, and exhibit a dusky red coloration. Its odor is reminiscent of fig leaves, and its taste is aromatic with a slight acrid quality. Historically, the contrayerva root was regarded by many authors as one of the most effective anti-epidemic remedies available. Dr. Nathaniel Hodges (1629–1688), in his treatise on the Great Plague of London (Loimologia, published in 1672), included a recipe that he claimed was highly successful in combating the plague. This recipe prominently featured the contrayerva root as one of its main ingredients.
